title: Official explanations: Mogul, balloons, flares and misidentification
notes: The case against, in one place. It shares Roswell's reports by design: a reader who opens the explanations should find them without going through the incident.

lead.text: The official explanations, gathered in one place: the Air Force's reports of 1994 to 1997 concluded that the Roswell debris most likely came from a Project Mogul balloon train and that the bodies accounts came from later test dummies and accidents, and a 1997 Air National Guard statement put the Phoenix lights down to flares. These are the conclusions of the offices that issued them; the board carries them as such.

summary.text: The Roswell reports were produced after Representative Steven Schiff pressed for records; Schiff also tasked the General Accounting Office, which searched from March 1994 to June 1995 and reported on 28 July 1995.

The first report, The Roswell Report: Fact versus Fiction in the New Mexico Desert, was the work of Col. Richard Weaver, the Air Force Secretary's director of security and special programme oversight, with 1st Lt. James McAndrew, who wrote its Project Mogul synopsis; the second, Case Closed (1997), is McAndrew's alone.
The Air Force volumes exist because Jesse Marcel's 1978 account restarted the case, and they conclude against him.

In the same pattern, a 2010 Brazilian military inquiry explained the Varginha vehicle movements as routine; on the board's reading, neither that inquiry nor the 1997 Air Force report published the underlying unit movement records.

record.text: The Air Force's July 1994 report concluded that the Army Air Forces did not recover an extraterrestrial vehicle and crew, after reviewing classified and unclassified holdings nationwide, and that the most likely source of the wreckage was one of the Project Mogul balloon trains, a then-classified top-priority programme of balloon-borne experiments.

The 1994 report attributed the debris to Mogul Flight No. 4, launched 4 June 1947 from Alamogordo, and acknowledged that the weather balloon account given in 1947 was a cover story; at the Secretary's written direction, former members and contract scientists were released from any nondisclosure agreements on the relevant classified work.

Case Closed concludes that many years of Air Force activity were consolidated into July 1947, that the aliens were probably anthropomorphic test dummies carried aloft by high-altitude balloons, that the unusual military activity was balloon launch and recovery, and that the hospital bodies accounts combine a 1956 KC-97 accident and a 1959 manned balloon mishap. It states that the bodies claims only became part of the incident after 1978.

Case Closed prints sworn statements from ten named Air Force personnel and full interview transcripts of five witnesses, including Glenn Dennis and James Ragsdale, whose words that they were using dummies it quotes in support.

On Dennis's missing nurse, the 1997 report uses morning reports and personnel records to show that a nurse of the name he gave never served, and identifies another nurse as matching every other particular.
It proposes that witnesses to the San Agustin claim may have confused the Plains with San Agustin Pass or Peak, near ranges where many dummy balloon flights ended.

GAO made no finding on the cause. It reported that its search yielded two records originating in 1947, that Roswell Army Air Field administrative records for 1945-1949 and outgoing messages for October 1946 to December 1949 were destroyed without any record of who destroyed them or under what authority, and that the CIA found no documents on the crash.

GAO also recorded that on 8 July 1947 an Eighth Air Force official told the FBI's Dallas office of a hexagonal disc suspended from a balloon that resembled a high-altitude weather balloon with a radar reflector; the same day Brig. Gen. Roger Ramey presented the debris at Fort Worth as a weather balloon.
AARO's 2024 historical report reaffirmed that the Roswell materials were consistent with a balloon of the type used in Project Mogul.

claimed.text: Marcel, the 509th's intelligence officer who handled the debris, said in 1978 that the weather balloon explanation was a cover story, that the material was not from a balloon or of terrestrial manufacture, and that the material shown at Fort Worth was substituted.

The Maryland Air National Guard's spokesman, Capt. Drew Sullins, said eight of its A-10s flew training missions over the Goldwater range on 13 March 1997 dropping high-intensity flares that fall slowly by parachute.

David Morehouse said on a podcast that the explanation at the time was Operation Snowbird, A-10 training from Davis-Monthan; those words appear nowhere in the opened record, and an alternative explanation offered on the same podcast has no federal award record behind it.

contested.text: Case Closed's own account puts the dummy tests principally between 1953 and 1959, years after July 1947, and the reports contradict Marcel, the officer who physically handled the material.

On the board's reading, Mogul cannot be checked against the base's own message traffic, because GAO found it destroyed without disposition authority, so the explanation rests on reconstruction rather than the contemporaneous record; the same destruction means Marcel's account cannot be checked either.

On the board's reading, an explanation that needs witnesses to have telescoped events of six to twelve years later into July 1947 is weaker than the one it replaced, and it came only under congressional pressure forty-seven years on.

The records disagree with each other over time: the 1947 weather balloon account was itself conceded in 1994 to have been a cover story, and on the board's reading the durable finding is an admitted false public account plus records destroyed without traceable authority.

On the board's reading, routing the inquiry to the director of security and special programme oversight, not to Air Force history or public affairs, suggests the department expected any material to sit in special access channels; the report's structure also tracks the witnesses introduced by Randle and Schmitt's books.
The flares explanation arrived four months after the event, dated 26 July 1997.

The witness record the reports answer is itself unsettled: Stringfield's seventh status report records a source placing the 1947 event just north of Roswell rather than on the Plains of San Agustin, and Randle has since said he is no longer sure what happened at Roswell.

questions: Who destroyed the Roswell Army Air Field message traffic for 1946-1949, when, and under what authority?
Was the Secretary's release from nondisclosure agreements a written instrument that could itself be requested?
Was material substituted between Roswell and Fort Worth on 8 July 1947?
Does any Ballard Funeral Home or base mortuary record from July 1947 bear on Dennis's casket enquiry?
Why did the Phoenix lights explanation take four months, and does any unit record of the 13 March 1997 sorties survive?
Would the Brazilian and US unit movement logs, if published, support the routine explanations?
Randle, Friedman, Schmitt and others reject Mogul outright: what record would settle it either way?
Carey and Schmitt record witnesses who say Dennis told them of the casket calls long before Roswell was a commercial subject; does any of those accounts predate 1978 in writing?
Ragsdale gave different crash-site locations in different statements: which, if any, is the earliest?
